scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Vayia Strose kai Louloudia originates from the island of Samos in Greece.
Its name, which translates to 'lay bay leaves and flowers' (Βάγια στρώστε και λουλούδια), derives from the work of the Samian poet Sideris Zisimou.
It developed as a regional folk expression performed during local festivities.
on_screen: Map: Greece · Europe
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed primarily during Apokries (Carnival) as well as informal social gatherings, the dance serves as a celebrated marker of Samian local culture, linking poetry, seasonal celebration, and community participation.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance shares structural and stylistic features with the traditional Syrtos.
Dancers begin in a circular formation structured into two lines.
At various intervals throughout the song, the participants move from two lines into a single line, and subsequently shift back into two lines.
Watch for Line Merge and Expansion.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Dancers form two lines inside a circle, merging into one single line and expanding back to two lines at musical intervals.
